strengths: Introduces a novel and intuitive framing of generation-understanding self-contradiction in unified MLLMs and proposes the Nonunified score to quantify it.
Shows that the understanding branch can act as an internal reward model for generation-targeted post-training, improving generation and unification without explicit external reward models.
Reports an interesting co-improvement effect in post-training and provides theoretical analysis via an extension of learning-dynamics theory to multimodal generation/understanding.

Highlights the risk of co-degradation under corrupted supervision, including the important observation that intrinsic metrics like Nonunified score cannot distinguish co-improvement from co-degradation.
Proposes a curriculum-based online post-training strategy and evaluates it on in-distribution and several out-of-distribution compositional generation tasks.
weaknesses: Empirical scope is limited: experiments primarily use Janus-Pro models and a single T2I-CompBench training subset (3D Spatial) with only 700 samples, so generalization across unified MLLM architectures and larger-scale benchmarks is not established.

Understanding improvements are small and may be statistically fragile: Table 1 shows net changes of only about 1% in many cases, WinRate excludes ties, and no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported.

The theoretical analysis is oversimplified relative to the method: it focuses on single-token SFT and a linear case with strong assumptions (uniform prompt prior, Bayes rule, single-token images), while the main experiments also use DPO and multi-token autoregressive image generation.

The claim of fine-tuning only the generation branch is ambiguous: if the autoregressive LLM/transformer parameters are shared with the understanding branch, co-improvement may partly follow from parameter sharing rather than the proposed aligned-dynamics mechanism.

Baselines and comparisons are incomplete or potentially unfair: T2I-R1 is compared despite using prompt augmentation/external rewards, whereas the proposed method avoids prompt expansion, and stronger external-reward or self-rewarding baselines are not thoroughly evaluated.
Curriculum results are mixed: CLO-SFT/CLO-DPO do not consistently outperform standard SFT/DPO across all OOD metrics, and some improvements are small or metric-specific.

The method is described as requiring no external signals, but external Qwen supervision is used for analysis, data-quality validation, and evaluation; the extent to which pure internal signals suffice is not fully demonstrated.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and details about architecture-specific fine-tuning, data construction, and statistical reliability are insufficient for full reproduction.

strengths: Identifies an interesting and plausible phenomenon of generation-understanding self-contradiction in unified MLLMs and proposes a simple quantitative metric, the Nonunified score.

Provides empirical analysis on Janus-Pro showing that most self-contradictions stem from weak generation rather than misunderstanding, motivating the use of the understanding branch as an internal reward.
Shows that standard post-training methods such as SFT and DPO with internal supervision can improve generation, unification, and some understanding performance.
Raises an important practical warning that internal metrics like Nonunified score can improve even under co-degradation, motivating external data-quality validation.
Extends a learning-dynamics framework to the multimodal generation-understanding setting and provides some empirical proxies consistent with the predicted co-improvement trend.
Proposes a curriculum-based online post-training strategy and reports some out-of-distribution improvements over standard DPO/SFT.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: using a model's own understanding branch as an internal reward, self-training, DPO/SFT, and curriculum learning for MLLMs are all existing ideas; the Nonunified score is a simple diagnostic rather than a fundamentally new method.

The central claim of self-improvement without external supervision is overstated: Qwen2.5-VL-72B is used as an oracle for analysis, evaluation, and suggested data-quality validation, so the framework is not fully self-contained.

Evaluation is narrow and insufficient for a top-tier conference: experiments mainly use Janus-Pro-1B/7B on one T2I-CompBench subset (3D Spatial) with 700 prompts, with few or no comparisons to other unified MLLMs, external-reward baselines, GRPO-style methods, or strong data-filtering baselines.
The paper lacks rigorous statistical evidence: no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; reported co-improvement ratios are very small and could be within noise.

The theory is weak relative to the claims: Proposition 1 relies on strong single-token, uniform-prior, Bayes-rule, and linear/softmax assumptions; the sign-consistency argument is heuristic, not a general guarantee, and is not directly derived for DPO.
The co-degradation evidence is based on an artificial corruption setting (fixed token ID) and mainly on the 1B model, so it is not yet strong evidence of a general failure mode.

Curriculum results are mixed and do not consistently support the claimed superiority: CLO-SFT worsens in-distribution Nonunified score compared with SFT, and several OOD understanding/unification results are worse than standard DPO/SFT.
The metric design is problematic: Nonunified score can improve under degradation, and WinRate excludes ties, so it can appear high even when only a small fraction of predictions change.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release, few hyperparameter details, no seed variance, and unclear compute/epoch parity between curriculum and non-curriculum methods.
Presentation has clarity issues: dense notation, unclear Figure 6 ratios, and overclaiming of consistent improvements despite mixed empirical results.

strengths: Introduces a clear and useful framing: quantifying generation-understanding self-contradiction via the Nonunified score and showing that most contradictions arise from weak generation rather than misunderstanding.

Demonstrates a practical self-improvement approach that uses the understanding branch as an internal reward signal for SFT/DPO, improving generation and unification without external reward models during training.
Reports and investigates a co-improvement effect between generation and understanding in post-training, supported by empirical analysis and a learning-dynamics theory extension.
Provides Proposition 1 and a case study linking generation and understanding updates, offering a principled explanation for both co-improvement and potential co-degradation.

Empirically validates the co-degradation risk under corrupted supervision and highlights an important limitation: internal metrics like the Nonunified score cannot distinguish co-degradation from co-improvement.

Proposes a curriculum-based online post-training strategy that dynamically incorporates harder prompts as model capabilities improve, with evaluations on in-distribution and multiple out-of-distribution T2I-CompBench tasks.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear takeaways and useful appendix details on training and analysis.
weaknesses: Experimental scope is limited: the main training and analysis focus on Janus-Pro-7B with only 700 samples from the 3D Spatial subset, leaving generalization across architectures, datasets, and larger-scale settings largely untested.

Evaluation and analysis depend heavily on Qwen2.5-VL-72B as an external oracle for WinRate and weak-generation/weak-understanding labels, so the self-improvement claim is only about the training signal, not a fully self-contained evaluation.

The theoretical analysis is restricted to single-token SFT and local NTK-style assumptions; it does not formally cover DPO or multi-token image generation, making the connection to practical algorithms more heuristic than complete.
Curriculum results are mixed: CLO-DPO/CLO-SFT do not consistently outperform standard SFT/DPO across all metrics and tasks, which weakens the claim of uniformly better unification and performance.

Baselines and comparisons are somewhat narrow: other relevant self-improvement/unification methods are discussed but not empirically compared, and the T2I-R1 comparison may not be fully apples-to-apples due to external rewards and prompt expansion.

No variance estimates, error bars, or significance tests are reported; metrics such as UniDet, WinRate, and Nonunified score can be noisy, and checkpoint selection based on the Nonunified score may introduce bias.

Novelty is moderate: generation-understanding mismatch and self-reward post-training have related precedents, and the main contribution is an empirical analysis plus curriculum strategy rather than a fundamentally new capability.

strengths: Introduces a simple, interpretable non-unification score to quantify the generation–understanding gap internally, and performs a broad empirical study across six MLLMs and multiple task difficulties.
Proposes an internal self-improvement framework that uses the model’s own understanding branch to score generations and construct SFT/DPO data, avoiding external reward models.
Reports improvements on T2I-CompBench++ and provides some evidence of co-improvement on understanding benchmarks and qualitative examples.
Connects the observed co-improvement effect to learning dynamics/eNTK theory, offering a plausible mechanistic perspective and motivating curriculum learning.
Includes useful implementation details, hyperparameters, and some ablations on which model components to update.
weaknesses: Major evaluation concern: the post-training data is constructed from T2I-CompBench++ prompts, and the main evaluation is also on T2I-CompBench++. The paper does not sufficiently describe a held-out split, so the central gains may reflect benchmark-specific fine-tuning or train/test overlap rather than generalizable self-improvement.

Generalization evidence is weak: on held-out benchmarks such as GenEval and Science-T2I, gains are small or mixed (e.g., GenEval overall generation 79.36→79.89, Science-T2I 24.49→25.07), which does not strongly support the broad claims of improved generation and unification.

Novelty is limited: using self-evaluation to filter or score generated data for SFT/DPO is intuitive and closely related to existing self-improvement/self-reward pipelines; the non-unification score is a straightforward self-consistency metric, and the curriculum-learning extension is also largely intuitive.

The theoretical analysis is not rigorous enough to substantiate the co-improvement explanation. It relies on an assumed dominance of a shared eNTK term, and the empirical validation uses prompt/image similarity as a proxy for eNTK rather than measuring the kernels directly. The link from eNTK alignment to the observed binary understanding improvement remains heuristic.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only two MLLMs (Janus-Pro-7B and Show-o) are self-improved, and most quantitative emphasis is on T2I-CompBench++. There is no statistical significance testing or confidence interval reporting, and the win-rate metric for understanding depends on Qwen as an external oracle while excluding ties, making it noisy.

Curriculum-learning improvements are often marginal or inconsistent: for Janus-Pro, overall unification changes only from 16.98 to 16.92; for Show-o, overall generation changes from 52.67 to 52.82 and understanding stays at 66.67, with some subtasks degrading. The claim of consistent gains across most tasks overstates the evidence.

Baselines such as T2I-R1 and HermesFlow rely on external rewards and may differ in training data/compute, so the comparison is not fully apples-to-apples. The paper also does not analyze failure cases or possible reward hacking from using the model’s own understanding as the scorer.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, and some data-construction and evaluation details are under-specified, particularly the exact train/test split for T2I-CompBench++ and the selection of evaluation prompts.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the generation-understanding gap in unified multimodal LLMs.
Provides a large-scale empirical verification of non-unification across six MLLMs and nine tasks, with stratification by task difficulty and some human checking.
Proposes a conceptually simple self-improvement framework that uses the stronger understanding branch to score generations and construct SFT/DPO data without external reward models.
Reports empirical improvements on T2I-CompBench++, GenEval, and Science-T2I for Janus-Pro and Show-o, including some gains over external-reward baselines.
Extends the approach with curriculum learning and shows adaptive data expansion from a discard pool, which is a reasonable practical addition.
Includes extensive appendices with implementation details, examples, and an attempt at a theoretical treatment.
weaknesses: The central theoretical explanation via shared eNTK is not convincingly established. The analysis assumes shared tokenizers, which does not directly match decoupled architectures like Janus-Pro, and the extension is hand-wavy. More importantly, the empirical validation uses input similarity as a proxy for eNTK Frobenius norms, which is not a valid proxy for gradient-based NTK quantities. No actual eNTK is computed, and the claimed dominance of shared terms is hypothesized rather than demonstrated.

The mathematics does not prove sign alignment between generation and understanding updates. The understanding dynamics include posterior weights and additional terms absent from the generation update, so the claimed alignment is not established beyond informal reasoning.

Evaluation relies heavily on Qwen2.5-VL-72B as an external oracle for both weak-generation analysis and win-rate evaluation. The win-rate metric excludes ties and does not report the number of disagreement cases, making high or low values hard to interpret. There is no human validation of the win-rate metric, and understanding benchmark gains are very small and likely within noise.

The co-improvement claim is weakly supported. Improvements on standard understanding benchmarks are marginal, and the main evidence comes from a win-rate metric that can be unstable when based on few disagreement samples. The paper therefore overstates the strength of the co-improvement effect.

The method may be circular and prone to reinforcing label noise, since it uses the same understanding branch to judge generations. The paper does not analyze this failure mode or compare against simple rejection sampling, filtering, self-rewarding, or other self-improvement baselines, so it is unclear how much the specific internal-gap framing contributes.

Experiments are limited to two MLLMs for self-improvement even though six MLLMs are evaluated in the phenomenon section. The paper does not show whether the method works on BAGEL, EMU3, VILA-U, or BLIP3-o, and data sizes are inconsistent across tables.
Some empirical results are mixed: DPO sometimes underperforms SFT, curriculum-learning gains are often marginal, and there are no statistical significance tests or variance estimates.

The non-unification metric is a binary self-consistency score that can be confounded by prompt ambiguity, answer calibration, and the exact scoring prompt. The weak-generation metric also depends on Qwen, and the human check shows large discrepancies on hard tasks, so the central diagnostic is less reliable than claimed.

Novelty is limited. Using an internal understanding branch as a reward/filter for generation is close to existing self-improvement, self-rewarding, and self-critique paradigms. Co-improvement is already known in pre-training, and the curriculum-learning extension is standard.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence: surpassing external-reward baselines holds only on selected metrics, the eNTK theory is decorative rather than validated, and the unification/co-improvement conclusions are not sufficiently isolated from simpler explanations.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. No code or data release is mentioned, exact weak-generation/win-rate dataset construction and disagreement counts are missing, and some hyperparameter/data-size reporting is inconsistent.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study across six unified MLLMs and nine tasks, confirming the widespread non-unification phenomenon and attributing it primarily to weak generation.

Introduces a simple yet effective internal-gap-based self-improvement framework that leverages the understanding branch to score generations, achieving significant gains in generation and unification without external signals.
Identifies and empirically demonstrates a co-improvement effect where generation-targeted self-improvement also enhances understanding, supported by win-rate evaluations and concrete examples.
Extends learning dynamics theory to the MLLM setting, providing a plausible eNTK-based explanation for co-improvement, with empirical evidence using similarity proxies.
Shows that curriculum learning can be integrated into self-improvement to reuse underutilized samples, further improving generation, understanding, and unification.
Compares against strong baselines that rely on external reward models (e.g., T2I-R1, HermesFlow) and shows competitive or superior performance, strengthening the practical relevance of the method.
Provides detailed implementation hyperparameters, data construction pipelines, and ablation studies, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: In Section 5.1, the likelihood definitions for generation and understanding appear to swap z_und and z_gen (generation uses softmax(z_und) and understanding uses softmax(z_gen)), which is inconsistent with the rest of the derivation and undermines the clarity and rigor of the theoretical presentation.

The eNTK-based explanation of co-improvement is not directly verified; the paper relies on text/image similarity proxies for eNTK rather than computing actual eNTK values, making the theoretical claim suggestive rather than conclusive.
Self-improvement experiments are validated on only two MLLMs (Janus-Pro-7B and Show-o), limiting the generalizability of the empirical claims.

The non-unification score is an internal self-consistency metric that may be partially circular: improving it could reflect better internal alignment rather than true prompt alignment, even though generation benchmarks and external judges partially mitigate this concern.
Understanding improvements on general understanding benchmarks (e.g., POPE) are mixed, with some metrics decreasing, which slightly weakens the claimed co-improvement effect.
Curriculum learning yields only modest additional gains over standard self-improvement, and the ablation on curriculum timing is limited.
The paper does not fully clarify potential train/test overlap between the prompts used for post-training data construction and the evaluation sets.
